questions.question: What is hoisting, and how does the temporal dead zone work?
questions.title: Hoisting and the temporal dead zone
questions.direct_answer: Hoisting is the observable result of declarations being processed when a scope is created. Function declarations are initialized with their function, var bindings with undefined, and let, const, and class bindings remain uninitialized until evaluation reaches their declaration. Access during that uninitialized interval is the temporal dead zone and throws ReferenceError.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether hoisting is explained as binding initialization rather than source movement.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying let and const are not hoisted at all.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Knowing typeof does not bypass a temporal-dead-zone binding.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Hoisting describes declaration setup before statement execution.
Function declarations are callable before their source line in the same scope.
var exists early with the value undefined.
let, const, and class exist early but remain uninitialized.
Reading an uninitialized lexical binding throws ReferenceError.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Hoisting is a useful name for the way JavaScript creates bindings before executing the statements in a scope. The declaration kind determines the binding's initial state, so saying that declarations simply move to the top is an incomplete mental model.

A function declaration is initialized with its function object during scope setup and can be called earlier in that scope. A `var` binding is initialized to `undefined`, so an early read succeeds but often hides a sequencing bug.

`let`, `const`, and class declarations are also known to the scope, but they are uninitialized until their declaration is evaluated. For example, reading `price` before `let price = 10` throws a `ReferenceError`; that source interval is the temporal dead zone. `typeof` also throws for a lexical binding in its temporal dead zone, unlike an undeclared name.

I declare values close to first use and avoid code that depends on early access. The rules matter most when explaining shadowing, default parameters, and cyclic initialization—not as permission to reorder declarations carelessly.

sections.title: Scope creation happens before statement execution
sections.content: The engine establishes declarations and then evaluates code in order. An initialized function or undefined var can be used immediately; an uninitialized lexical binding cannot.

sections.title: The temporal dead zone protects initialization order
sections.content:
A lexical name shadows an outer name throughout its block, including before its own declaration. An early reference therefore reaches the inner uninitialized binding rather than falling back to the outer value. This prevents code from observing a partially initialized lexical variable.

`const` must have an initializer in an ordinary declaration because its binding cannot later be assigned. A `let` declaration without an initializer becomes `undefined` when its declaration statement runs, not at scope entry.

sections.title: Binding state before its declaration line
sections.content:
| Declaration | Binding exists? | Initialized value | Early read |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Function declaration | Yes | Function object | Works |
| `var` | Yes | `undefined` | Works |
| `let` / `const` / class | Yes | Uninitialized | `ReferenceError` |

questions.question: What are global, function, block, and module scope in JavaScript?
questions.title: JavaScript scope types
questions.direct_answer: Global scope is the outer environment of a script, function scope belongs to a function call, block scope is created for lexical declarations inside structures such as braces, and module scope is private to an ES module. var follows function/global scope, while let, const, class, and import bindings follow lexical block or module scope.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether declaration kind and execution context are mapped to scope.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming scope and object lifetime are the same thing.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguishing browser script globals from ES module bindings.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: var is scoped to the nearest function or global script environment.
let, const, and class are scoped to the nearest lexical block.
Each function call creates bindings for parameters and locals.
Top-level ES module declarations are not global object properties.
Modules are strict by default and expose values only through exports.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Scope defines where a binding can be resolved. A function call creates a function environment for parameters and local declarations, while a block can create an additional environment for `let`, `const`, and class declarations.

For example, a `let` declared inside an `if` block cannot be read after the closing brace, but a `var` declared there belongs to the surrounding function. A `var` inside a function still does not escape into the caller.

Top-level scripts and ES modules differ. At top level of a classic browser script, `var` can create a property on the global object; top-level `let` and `const` do not. Every ES module has its own module scope, runs in strict mode, and shares only explicit exports and imports.

Narrow scope reduces accidental coupling and shortens the region in which a name can change. I prefer block-scoped declarations and modules, while recognizing that scope controls name visibility—not object lifetime by itself. A reachable closure can keep a scoped value alive after its block or function has finished.

sections.title: Scope is visibility; reachability controls lifetime
sections.content: Leaving a block prevents later lexical name lookup, but garbage collection depends on whether any reachable object or closure still refers to the value.

sections.title: Global environment has two kinds of top-level binding
sections.content:
Browser scripts have an object record associated with the global object and a declarative record for lexical declarations. This is why `var answer = 42` can appear as `window.answer`, while `let answer = 42` does not.

Modules avoid that shared namespace and evaluate once per resolved module instance. Imports are live bindings, so an importer observes later updates made by the exporting module but cannot assign to the imported binding.

sections.title: Where declarations live
sections.content:
| Context | `var` | `let` / `const` / class |
|---|---|---|
| Function body | Function scope | Function/block scope |
| Nested block | Surrounding function | That block |
| Browser script top level | Global object binding | Global lexical binding |
| ES module top level | Module scope | Module scope |

questions.question: What is variable shadowing, and when can it cause bugs?
questions.title: Variable shadowing
questions.direct_answer: Shadowing occurs when an inner scope declares a binding with the same name as an outer binding, so references in the inner scope resolve to the inner one. It is legal and sometimes useful, but similar names can hide an intended update, create temporal-dead-zone errors, or make nested code hard to read.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether shadowing follows lexical lookup and scope boundaries.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing a nested declaration with same-scope redeclaration.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Using semantic names to prevent an intended outer update from being hidden.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: An inner binding with the same name hides the outer binding in that scope.
Shadowing follows lexical name resolution and is not object-property overriding.
The inner lexical binding shadows even before its declaration line.
A parameter can shadow a module or outer-function variable.
Rename values when identical names represent different concepts.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Variable shadowing happens when a nested scope declares the same name as an enclosing scope. Inside the nested scope, normal lexical lookup finds the inner binding first, so the outer one is temporarily inaccessible by that name.

For example, a function may have an outer `status`, then a block declares `const status = response.status`. Logging `status` inside the block refers to the response status; code after the block again sees the outer value.

Shadowing is not always wrong. A short callback parameter such as `item` may clearly represent the current item even when another unrelated scope used the same word. It becomes risky when the names represent different concepts, when a programmer intended to assign the outer state, or when nesting makes the active binding hard to identify.

A lexical declaration shadows for its entire block, including its temporal dead zone, so reading the name before the declaration does not fall back to the outer value—it throws. I keep nested scopes small and rename semantically different values, such as `httpStatus` and `jobStatus`, rather than relying on indentation to explain them.

sections.title: Nearest lexical binding wins
sections.content: Name resolution stops at the first matching environment. Once an inner binding exists, there is no syntax for selecting an outer local binding with the same name; a clearer name or refactoring is required.

sections.title: Shadowing differs from redeclaration
sections.content:
A separate nested environment may legally declare the same name. Declaring `let` twice in the same lexical scope is a syntax error. `var` declarations share their function scope, so repeated `var` is redeclaration rather than block shadowing.

Properties belong to objects, not lexical environments. A subclass method overriding a prototype method and a local variable shadowing an outer variable may look similar in source, but they use different lookup systems.

sections.title: Resolving a shadowed name
sections.content:
inside block: find inner `status` → stop
after block: inner environment is gone
find outer `status` → use outer binding

sections.title: Use distinct names for distinct meanings
